summary: Describes why quality of service and media authorization are needed in SIP and defines a private extension that ties QoS admission control to call signaling. It helps guard against denial of service attacks. It applies only within administrative domains, or federations of them, that have agreed on policies in advance.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3313 adds a private SIP header so that a phone network can approve a call before it reserves priority bandwidth for it. The proxy that handles the call issues a token, and the phone presents that token when it asks for the bandwidth, so a flood of unauthorised calls cannot take priority service. It works only inside one organisation's network, or among networks that already share one policy.

subtitle: How a SIP proxy approves a call before the network reserves priority bandwidth for it

tldr.problem: Bandwidth on an IP network is limited, so a network must decide which calls may receive priority service. Without that decision, unauthorised requests can crowd out real calls and deny service.
tldr.mechanism: A QoS-enabled SIP proxy checks the caller and asks a policy controller for a media authorization token, then returns the token to the phone in a new P-Media-Authorization header. The phone presents that token to the network when it asks for bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: The extension lets an operator control how much reserved bandwidth is given out and makes IP telephony harder to attack, but it works only inside one administrative domain or a federation of domains that already agree on policy, and it needs message bodies to stay readable to the proxy.

facts.label: Token contents
facts.value: A Policy-Element from RFC 2750, without Length but with P-Type

facts.label: Example deployments
facts.value: DOCSIS cable networks and 3G wireless networks

facts.label: Applicable scope
facts.value: One administrative domain, or a federation of domains with agreed policies

today: RFC 3313 is an Informational memo published in January 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the description of this private SIP header. The document says the extension applies only inside one administrative domain, or among domains that have already agreed on policy, and that it is generally incompatible with encrypting message bodies end to end.

sections.title: Scope of Applicability
sections.content:
RFC 3313 defines a private extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), the text-based protocol that sets up a call. The extension lets a network decide whether a call may receive reserved bandwidth before the call carries any media.

The mechanism works only inside one administrative domain, or among administrative domains that have already agreed on a common policy. Both the proxy that authorizes the QoS and the policy control of the network that provides the QoS must belong to that domain or federation of domains. The document is explicit that this is not a solution for the Internet at large, because general Internet practice separates data transport from applications.

Because the proxy has to read the message bodies that describe the media streams, the extension is generally incompatible with encrypting those bodies end to end. The document names DOCSIS-based cable networks and third-generation (3G) wireless networks as the kind of access network where such a deployment exists, and describes a closed network that emulates a traditional circuit-switched telephone network as the example case.
sections.plainLanguage: This extension lets a phone network approve a call before it reserves special bandwidth for it. It works only inside one organisation's network, or among networks that already share one policy, because the proxy has to read the call's media description.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
End-to-end bandwidth is not unlimited. QoS gives preferential treatment to one flow at the expense of another, so the document argues that some form of policy control is needed over who receives that treatment. The result is fairness in the sharing of capacity, and it also prevents denial of service attacks, because a flood of requests cannot all claim priority.

The architecture has three named parts. A SIP user agent (UA) sits at the edge of a QoS-enabled network. An edge router acts as a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), the device that puts the network's decisions into effect. A QoS-enabled SIP proxy sits between them and is the party that can talk to the network's policy control, a Policy Decision Point (PDP).

The UA is assumed to need an authorization token to obtain quality of service. It gets that token over SIP from the QoS-enabled proxy, in a header this document defines. The proxy in turn speaks either directly to the edge router or to a PDP to obtain a suitable token for the UA.
sections.plainLanguage: Bandwidth is limited, and giving one call priority takes capacity from another. So a network needs a rule about who gets priority, and a way to stop anyone claiming priority without that rule.

sections.title: Overview of a Session
sections.content:
The overview gives the shape of a session that needs reserved bandwidth. The user agent sends an INVITE to the QoS-enabled proxy. For each dialog that results, the proxy includes one or more media authorization tokens in all unreliable provisional responses except 100, in the first reliable 1xx or 2xx response, and in all retransmissions of that reliable response for the dialog.

When the user agent asks for QoS, it includes the media authorization tokens with the resource reservation. The reservation mechanism is not part of SIP and is not described in this document. A user agent may also receive an INVITE from its QoS-enabled proxy that already carries tokens, and it presents those in the same way when it asks for QoS.

The worked example in section 6 shows the token travelling with an RSVP reservation. The originating proxy stores the authorized media description, gets a token that points at that description from the originating Policy Decision Point, and puts the token in the P-Media-Authorization header of a response. The user agent copies the token into its RSVP messages as a Policy-Element, and the edge router checks it with the policy controller before forwarding the reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: The call starts with the usual SIP request. The proxy answers with permission to use reserved bandwidth attached to the call, and the phone sends that permission on when it asks for the bandwidth. The reservation itself is a separate mechanism that this document does not define.

sections.title: The P-Media-Authorization Header
sections.content:
The extension adds one SIP header field, P-Media-Authorization. It carries one or more media authorization tokens, and those tokens are what the user agent passes to the separate resource reservation mechanism to show that QoS was authorized for the media flows of the session.

The grammar of the header is short. The field name, a colon, one token, and any number of further tokens separated by commas. A token is one or more hexadecimal digits.

The document extends the tables that show where each SIP header may appear with an entry for the new field, giving its placement for requests and responses including ACK, BYE, CANCEL, INVITE, OPTIONS, REGISTER, INFO, PRACK, UPDATE, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. The field can be used only in SIP requests or responses that can carry a SIP offer or answer, which keeps its scope narrow.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy passes the permission along in a new SIP header called P-Media-Authorization. Each value in that header is a short block of hexadecimal digits that stands for the approved media description.

sections.title: Procedures for Proxies and User Agents
sections.content:
The document gives the rules for each party. The user agent client should authorize the initial INVITE, the mid-call messages that result in network QoS resource changes, and any mid-call change in call destination, by sending them through the QoS-enabled proxies. It should use all the tokens from the most recent request or response that carried the header, both for the first reservation and for later refresh reservation messages. A reservation function within the user agent converts each string of hex digits into binary and uses each result as a Policy-Element as defined in RFC 2750, excluding Length but including P-Type, which is included in each token. Those Policy-Elements typically contain the authorizing entity and credentials.

The originating proxy authenticates the caller and verifies that the caller is authorized to receive QoS. Working with an originating Policy Decision Point, it obtains or generates one or more tokens, and it must add the P-Media-Authorization header to all unreliable provisional responses except 100, to the first reliable 1xx or 2xx response, and to retransmissions of that response, when the response may result in network QoS changes. A response with an SDP description may result in such changes.

The destination proxy verifies that the called party is authorized to receive QoS, obtains or generates a token in the same way with a terminating Policy Decision Point, and must add the header to the request it sends to the user agent server if that message may result in network QoS changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each party has a job. The phones send their call setup through the proxy that checks whether the call may have priority bandwidth. The proxy checks the caller, asks the policy controller for a token, and puts that token in the SIP messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A QoS-enabled proxy should authenticate the user agent before it provides it with a media authorization token. The method and the policy for that authentication are outside the scope of the document, which notes that it could for example be done with the standard SIP authentication mechanisms.

Media authorization tokens sent in the P-Media-Authorization header MUST be protected from eavesdropping and tampering, which can be done for example through IPSec or TLS. That gives only hop-by-hop security. If one or more intermediaries such as proxies sit between the user agent and the QoS-enabled proxy, those intermediaries have access to the header value, which compromises its confidentiality and integrity and enables both theft-of-service and denial-of-service attacks against the user agent.

Consequently the header MUST NOT be available to any untrusted intermediary in the clear or without integrity protection. The document states that there is currently no mechanism in SIP that would satisfy these requirements, so proxies MUST NOT send P-Media-Authorization headers through untrusted intermediaries. It adds that S/MIME-based encryption in SIP is not available to proxy servers, because proxies are not allowed to add message bodies.

Because the QoS-enabled proxy may need to inspect the message bodies that describe the media streams, such bodies should not be encrypted. That removes end-to-end confidentiality for them and lowers the overall security possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy should check who the caller is before it issues a token, and the tokens must be protected in transit. But that protection only covers one hop, so a proxy in the middle could steal or change them. The document therefore tells proxies not to pass the header through intermediaries they do not trust.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: The calling phone starts the call.

messages.label: AuthProfile
messages.note: The proxy sends the media description it wants approved.

messages.label: AuthToken
messages.note: The policy controller stores that description and returns a token pointing at it.

messages.label: 18x response
messages.note: The token travels in the P-Media-Authorization header.

messages.label: RSVP-PATH
messages.note: The phone sends the token as a Policy-Element with its path request.

messages.label: COPS request
messages.note: The edge router asks the policy controller whether the token is valid.

messages.label: Install decision
messages.note: The policy controller confirms the authorization.

messages.label: RSVP-PATH
messages.note: The path request continues on to the other end.
